title: Preface by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati
html:
Preface (bhumika) to Sri Chaitanya-mangala1

The reader's qualification. In taking up any book one must first of all make the mind [pure and calm], not allow former impressions to prevail, and set about reading without prejudice, in a mood favourable to grasping its meaning. Every author wishes his labour to serve to free the reader from ignorance. On the other hand, the reader too, having considered his own qualification (adhikara), should think: "[I wish to read this book] in order to receive light on what I do not know." The pride nursed by lovers of argument, who, regarding themselves as examiners, set out to test the author, is merely the attitude of a trader. If one seeks in reading a calculation of profit, the place [of the truth] is taken by hopes of gain, honour and fame. Worldly people, thus driven by their desires, take the subject the book speaks of for merchandise — and are deprived of [the benefit borne by] the words of the devotee author.

The meaning of the book's title. By the pastimes of Sri Chaitanyadeva the bonds will fall from the living beings bewildered by maya and blessing (mangala) will come — therefore the narrative of Sri Chaitanya is called Sri Chaitanya-mangala. Sri Chaitanyadeva Himself is full of the highest blessing; therefore the narrative of Sri Chaitanya may well be called Chaitanya-mangala. Srila Vrindavana Dasa Thakura too wrote a book under this name; Srila Krishnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami Prabhu mentions it in his Sri Chaitanya-charitamrita2. That very book became famous under the name Sri Chaitanya-bhagavata.

Certain literati of Buddhist leanings and scholars attached to them have recently composed, in the guise of a literary monument, a fictitious book, and are trying to prove that it is old. [Certain] Shaiva literati and literati of [other] communities [hostile to bhakti], showing aversion to pure bhakti, have conceived the idea of uprooting pure bhakti by spreading [this book]. [The book] which mundane literati hostile to bhakti pass off as approved by devotees — displaying only contemptible efforts — we do not honour. Because of their Buddhist convictions and godlessness they have no access to the highest goal (paramartha); and the fruit of their illegitimate efforts, rooted in the desire to pass off the worthless (anartha) as the highest goal, is that the fictitious Chaitanya-mangala composed by Jayananda has been called into being3. Pure devotees never read such a book and do not, [by accepting it,] bring defilement on themselves. In the Bhakti-ratnakara and other books of Sri Narahari Chakravarti there is not a single mention of the Chaitanya-mangala of Jayananda and similar books; therefore, [regarding] this book contrary to the truth as the work of a deviant community (apasampradaya), we have given it the name A-chaitanya-mangala4. The admirers of such books may, together with the haters of bhakti, agree to support it, but we pay them our respects from afar.

In studying the life of Sri Chaitanya, let the indisputable books for us be the works of the reliable biographers of Sri Chaitanya — Srila Kavi-karnapura Gosvami, Srila Murari Gupta Vaidya, Srila Krishnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami and Srila Vrindavana Dasa Thakura. In the Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya, in the Gaura-krishnodaya of the Utkala poet Sri Govinda-deva, in Sri Chaitanya-mangala and [similar] books there is no glaring trace of doctrines opposed to bhakti, and therefore those who walk the path of bhakti accept them as evidence without hesitation5. But the Baul-chandrika, the [Bhakta]mala of Laladasa6, the Chaitanya-mangala of Jayananda and some other books, although they are now the chief object of study among literati, are untouchable for us […]: walking the path of bhakti, we dare not accept them. Those who have realized even a little of the nature of bhakti do not leave the path of bhakti, and so in their writings there is no place for the doctrine of the Charvakas, Buddhist beliefs or the dominance of materialism.

Seeing the grace of language of Srila Lochana Dasa Thakura's Sri Chaitanya-mangala and his heartfelt love for Sri Gaura, some indeed say that he is inclined to stray somewhat from the truth of pure bhakti. We are not prepared to say so, for "the actions and gestures of a Vaishnava are not understood even by the wise"7. May the abominable desire to impute the stench of the Gaura-nagari doctrine to Sri Chaitanya-mangala never take hold of our hearts8.

Our one hope with regard to the readers is that, praying to Sri Chaitanya for mercy, we shall be freed from various considerations full of anarthas and attain blessing. We also hope that the readers will kindly not make common cause with the ten or thirteen deviant communities (apasampradayas) who come forward claiming to be called Gaudiyas and offend the feet of the true Gaudiyas9.

The source of Sri Chaitanya-mangala is the Sri Chaitanya-charita of Sri Murari Gupta. The author writes in the Sutra-khanda:

"All that the Lord did from His birth in childhood,
how from beginning to end He spread prema —
about all this Damodara Pandita questioned him,
and he told him everything from beginning to end in order.
Thus came about the book of Gauranga's deeds, composed in verse —
the dialogue with Damodara that came from Murari's lips.
Hearing it, I was filled with love,
and I tell of Gaura's deeds in a sung narrative, a panchali."10

The author of this book is a disciple of Srila Narahari Dasa, an associate of Sri Gaura; he was born in a vaidya family of the Rarh country, at Kogram in the Katwa subdivision of Burdwan district. In many places of the book Thakura Lochana Dasa calls himself a follower of Srila Narahari Sarakara Thakura Mahashaya.

Sri Chaitanya-mangala is a book of the panchali kind, that is, a work composed in song-metres of five kinds11. Its language shows an abundance of feeling and extraordinary grace. The collections of popular songs that have lately come into circulation under the name "Lochana's panchali" must be approached with special caution: into many of them the stench of the newfangled Gaura-nagari doctrine has been introduced.

Many hesitate to accept the historical statements of Sri Chaitanya-mangala: part [of them] has been gathered on the basis of dreams12, and full regard for the truth of pure bhakti is not seen everywhere. Tradition says that Srila Lochana Dasa Thakura's book was written somewhat before the Sri Chaitanya-bhagavata of Thakura Srila Vrindavana Dasa; when Srila Vrindavana's mother said that [that] book had been written earlier, it became necessary to rename the book of Sri Vrindavana Dasa Thakura13. No one can doubt the reliability of the geographical indications of Sri Chaitanya-mangala. The composition of Sri Chaitanya-mangala was begun on the basis of the childhood pastimes of Sri Gaurasundara recorded by Sri Murari Gupta Vaidya in the Sri Chaitanya-charita: Lochana Dasa took them as his source-evidence. The clear description in this book of Sri Chaitanyadeva's ideal of renunciation will give joy to the reader, and above all Srila Lochana Thakura's love for Sri Gaura will draw the love of Gaura's devotees — of this there is no doubt. The old panchali poetry of Gunaraja Khan was composed long before this book14. The songs of Sri Chaitanya-mangala are sung to this day in various places of Rarh, as jhumur or the songs of the Ramayana are sung. The poetry of Sri Chaitanya-charitamrita, founded on Srila Kaviraja Gosvami's description of prema-bhakti, the charming verse of Sri Lochana Dasa Thakura, and the supremely magnanimous grace of language of Sri Vrindavana Dasa Thakura, rooted in pure bhakti, have always increased the bliss of the devotees of Sri Gaura.

Notes

  1. Before the preface the edition has the title page and a guru-parampara in verse (the succession of teachers from Krishna and Brahma through Madhva, Madhavendra Puri and Ishvara Puri to Sri Chaitanya and onward, down to Bhaktivinoda Thakura and Gaurakishora Dasa Babaji); after the preface, an alphabetical index of the Sanskrit verses quoted in the poem and a list of the scriptures quoted. These we do not translate. The OCR text of the preface is damaged in places: what is restored by sense is given in square brackets, what is unreadable is marked […]. The bold subheadings are in the edition.
  2. E.g. Chaitanya-charitamrita, Adi 8.34: "Vrindavana Dasa wrote the Chaitanya-mangala."
  3. Jayananda is the author of a Chaitanya-mangala, a life of the Lord found in manuscripts and first published at the beginning of the twentieth century. Bhaktisiddhanta regards this book as unreliable and contrary to siddhanta; among other things it tells of the Lord's departure from a wound in the foot (cf. en/52, footnote 10). We render his judgement as it stands.
  4. A-chaitanya-mangala is a play on words: "not-Chaitanya-mangala", a book alien to Chaitanya and bringing no blessing.
  5. The Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya is a Sanskrit poem by Kavi-karnapura. The Gaura-krishnodaya is a Sanskrit poem by Govinda, a poet of Utkala (Orissa). Sri Chaitanya-mangala here is apparently Lochana Dasa's poem itself.
  6. The OCR reads «তমাল»; probably «ভক্তমাল», the Bhaktamala of Laladasa. The words that follow are unreadable. The Baul-chandrika is apparently a work of the Baul community, one of those Bhaktisiddhanta counts as deviant (apasampradayas).
  7. Chaitanya-charitamrita, Madhya 23.39: "The words, actions and gestures of one in whose heart prema for Krishna has arisen are not understood even by the wise."
  8. Gaura-nagari (gaura-nagari-vada) is the doctrine that worships Gaura as a nagara, the lover of women, after the pattern of Krishna and the gopis; the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, following Vrindavana Dasa and Krishnadasa Kaviraja, reject it. On Lochana Dasa's own lines in this vein see en/09, footnote 9, and en/18, footnotes 5–6.
  9. According to the list well known in the Gaudiya Math, the thirteen apasampradayas are: aul, baul, kartabhaja, nera, darvesh, sani, sahajiya, sakhibheki, smarta, jat-gosani, ativadi, chudadhari and gauranga-nagari.
  10. Sutra-khanda, vv. 53–56 (en/01); the translation is the same as there.
  11. The OCR reads «পচপ্রকার»; we read «পঞ্চপ্রকার», "of five kinds". Bhaktisiddhanta does not explain which five metres are meant.
  12. We read «স্বপ্নমূলে» ("on the basis of dreams"; the OCR has «স্বপ্রমূলে»); the reading is not entirely certain.
  13. The tradition is usually told thus: Vrindavana Dasa's book was at first called Chaitanya-mangala and was renamed Chaitanya-bhagavata when Lochana Dasa's poem of the same name appeared; Vrindavana Dasa's mother, Narayani, figures in the story. Bhaktisiddhanta's text is damaged here, and the sense is given according to the most probable reading. In scholarly literature Lochana Dasa's poem is usually dated later than the Chaitanya-bhagavata.
  14. Gunaraja Khan (Maladhara Basu) is the author of the Sri Krishna-vijaya (1470s), a Bengali retelling of the Bhagavata; the Lord praised his book (Chaitanya-charitamrita, Madhya 15.99–100).
